title: Electric Force and Coulomb's Law
seo_title: Coulomb's Law Worksheets: Electric Charge and Electric Force (High School Physics)
standard_text: Use mathematical representations of Newton's Law of Gravitation and Coulomb's Law to describe and predict the gravitational and electrostatic forces between objects.
meta_desc: Free high school physics worksheets on electric force (NGSS HS-PS2-4): like and unlike charges, Coulomb's law, the inverse-square law and counting electrons. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: F = kq₁q₂/r²: bigger charges, bigger force; twice the distance, 1/4 the force.
body_html:
How to think about it

Like charges repel, unlike charges attract: F = kq1q2 ÷ r2.

  • Double one charge → double the force. Double the distance → 1/4 the force.
  • Objects get charged when electrons move. Gaining electrons → negative; losing → positive.
  • k = 8.99 × 109 N·m²/C²; electric forces are much stronger than gravity between small particles.
Example

Both charges doubled, distance doubled?

2 × 2 ÷ 2²

Answer: the same size

Example

Gained 5 electrons. Charge?

5 × 1.6 × 10−19

Answer: −8.00 × 10−19 C

Common mistakes

  • Thinking protons move when objects are charged.
  • Thinking doubling the distance halves the force.
  • Thinking electric force is weaker than gravity.

faq.a: The electric force between two charges is F = kq₁q₂/r². It is larger for bigger charges and smaller at larger distances.
Electrons move from one object to another. The object that gains electrons becomes negative, and the one that loses them becomes positive.

faq.q: How are electric and gravitational forces alike?
faq.a: Both follow an inverse-square law. Unlike gravity, the electric force can attract or repel.
